title: A missing theorem on dual spaces

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 3.3, proof part (1), sentence defining the predual map J
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states: "Let J : X → X be the predual map of L_i. It is easy to see by duality theory that J² = I (since (J²)* = -I)." This is a sign contradiction. If (J²)* = -I on the dual, then separation by the dual implies J² = -I, not I. The subsequent argument itself requires J² = -I in order to invoke the stated complex-structure criterion. The later assertion that sI+tJ has inverse sI-tJ also holds when J²=-I (and s²+t²=1), not when J²=I. This must be corrected because it is central to the proof that X acquires complex structure.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proposition 2.3, proof, assertion that T : Min_R(X) → Min_C(Y) is completely contractive
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof says that because φ∘T is a contractive real functional for φ∈Ball(Y†), "it is clear that T : Min_R(X) → Min_C(Y) is a complete contraction." This does not follow: real scalar functionals control the real minimal matrix norms, whereas the complex minimal target norm is tested by complex-valued functionals. In fact the asserted intermediate map is false even for T=id on C. Let Z=[[1,i],[i,-1]]∈M_2(C). In Min_R(C), its norm is sup_θ ||Re(e^{iθ}Z)||=1, while in Min_C(C) its norm is the ordinary complex operator norm ||Z||=2. Thus id:Min_R(C)→Min_C(C) is not completely contractive. Consequently the displayed proof of Proposition 2.3 is invalid, and Proposition 2.3 is later used in the proof of Theorem 4.1 to assert that q is completely contractive.

Theorem 3.3 has only hypotheses: "Let X be ... Let Y=X† with this complex operator space structure," and states no conclusion at all. Nevertheless its proof is divided into "(1)" and then proceeds to establish several distinct conclusions about a complex structure on X, a complex predual W, and equivalent operator-space norms; later text refers to "Theorem 3.3 (3)." Since neither parts (1)–(3) nor their conclusions appear in the theorem statement, the result being proved and subsequently invoked is undefined. This is not merely cosmetic: later claims, including the discussion before Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.4, rely on knowing exactly which asserted conclusions of Theorem 3.3 are available.
